title: A Pattern Two Centuries Old: Backing the Opposition, Denying It Officially
hook: In 1805 a Venezuelan revolutionary asked Jefferson for help overthrowing Spanish rule. Jefferson denied involvement but quietly let him go — a pattern historians trace to 2026.
key_points: In 1805, Venezuelan revolutionary Francisco de Miranda asked President Jefferson for U.S. backing to overthrow Spanish colonial rule; Jefferson publicly denied involvement while letting Miranda depart with tacit encouragement and a privately-outfitted ship.
The 1806 expedition failed — Spanish forces captured and executed several participants — but Miranda escaped and later helped lead Venezuela's independence movement.

Historian Lindsay Schakenbach Regele argues this established a recurring U.S. pattern: cultivating foreign opposition figures, offering support while maintaining official deniability, and leveraging local allies for U.S. strategic interests.

She draws a direct parallel to 2026, when the Trump administration moved against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and backed opposition leader María Corina Machado, winner of the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize.
Both episodes reflect the same underlying tension in foreign policy: supporting regime change abroad while avoiding the appearance — and the direct legal responsibility — of an official act of war.
content_html: Historian Lindsay Schakenbach Regele traces, in The Conversation, a pattern in U.S. foreign policy toward Latin America that is nearly 250 years old: back opposition figures seeking to overthrow a government you oppose, but avoid officially claiming the intervention.
extra_html: In 1805, Venezuelan revolutionary Francisco de Miranda traveled to the U.S. to ask President Jefferson for backing to overthrow Spanish colonial rule. Jefferson publicly denied any U.S. involvement — while quietly letting Miranda leave New York with a privately-outfitted vessel and about 200 men. The 1806 expedition failed; Spanish forces captured and executed several participants, though Miranda escaped and went on to help lead Venezuela's later independence movement. Regele argues the episode set a template that recurs: cultivate a foreign opposition figure, provide support while preserving official deniability, and let local allies advance U.S. strategic interests on the ground. She draws a direct line to 2026, when the Trump administration moved against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and backed opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner and a longtime Maduro critic. Two centuries apart, both episodes turn on the same tension: pursuing regime change abroad while sidestepping the legal and diplomatic weight of openly declaring it. (This card describes U.S. policy toward Latin America specifically.)

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Lindsay Schakenbach Regele, Associate Professor of History, Miami University

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: Soft Power & Hard Power
related.hook: States get their way two ways: by force and money, or by attraction. Knowing the difference between hard power and soft power explains a lot about how influence really works.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

flashcards.prompt: What did Francisco de Miranda ask President Jefferson for in 1805, and how did Jefferson respond?
flashcards.back_html: Miranda sought U.S. backing to overthrow Spanish rule in Venezuela. Jefferson publicly denied involvement while quietly letting him leave with a privately-outfitted ship and tacit encouragement.

flashcards.prompt: What recurring pattern does historian Lindsay Schakenbach Regele identify across U.S. interventions in Latin America?

choices.text: Cultivating foreign opposition figures and offering support while maintaining official deniability
Declaring war formally through Congress before every intervention
Refusing any involvement with foreign opposition movements

flashcards.explanation_html: The through-line she traces is support paired with deniability, not formal, declared war — from Miranda in 1805 to Venezuela in 2026.

flashcards.prompt: Why would a government prefer 'deniable' support for foreign regime change over open, declared involvement?

choices.text: It can pursue strategic goals abroad while avoiding the legal and diplomatic responsibility of an official act of war
International law requires all support for foreign movements to be secret
It has no real difference in consequences for the government

flashcards.explanation_html: Deniability lets a state pursue influence abroad while sidestepping the formal accountability — legal and diplomatic — that comes with an acknowledged act of war.
